You are comparing two drafts written from the same brief. Read no other file, and do not run commands or browse; judge only the text below.

Brief: Write the README's opening paragraph and its Install and update section for the `tidy-hooks` plugin.

<<<DRAFT A
`tidy-hooks` is a Claude and Codex plugin that blocks `git commit` when staged files contain merge markers. If Node.js is missing, the hook fails open and commits proceed.

## Install and update

### Claude

Install:

```sh
claude plugin marketplace add example/tidy
claude plugin install tidy-hooks@tidy
```

Update:

```sh
claude plugin update tidy-hooks@tidy
```

### Codex

Install:

```sh
codex plugin marketplace add example/tidy
codex plugin add tidy-hooks@tidy
```

Codex skips plugin hooks until you review and trust them.

Update:

```sh
codex plugin marketplace upgrade tidy
```

Then restart Codex.
DRAFT A>>>

items.title: Thinking
items.text:
I'm weighing the two versions against each other. One says the hook fails open and commits still go through, which is more precise but a bit jargony, while the other just says commits proceed. I'm also checking where the trust note sits relative to the install command, since the ordering affects when a reader realizes they need to trust the plugin.

Weighing the two versions on whether the reader gets it. The "To update:" versus "To update, run:" labels are inconsistent in one of them, which counts against it, while the other's trust note sits right after the install step where it actually applies. Neither spells out how to trust hooks, so on reader clarity they come out about even, and I'm leaning toward the first version overall.

{"reader": "SAME", "careful": "A", "overall": "A", "reason": "Both drafts give the same working commands, but A keeps its labels consistent and puts the Codex trust note right after install, where it applies, while B adds lead-in lines that repeat the commands and words its two update labels differently."}
